newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders worry about job creation, pledge action.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders worry about job creation, pledge action.

text.p: European Union leaders said on Saturday they were deeply worried about the slow pace of job creation in the region and pledged firm action to combat unemployment.
At their summit in Dublin, the leaders of the 15-member bloc issued a declaration saying that the EU would give maximum support to member states in their efforts to promote employment.
"The need for firm and sustained action has never been greater," the leaders said in their Dublin Declaration on Employment, describing job creation as the EU's greatest challenge.

"While in the Union as a whole, there has been a slight increase in employment over the past year, the European Council (leaders) remains deeply concerned at the slow pace of progress," the declaration said.
The EU's unemployment rate, at about 10.8 percent,is roughly twice that in the United States.
However, the leaders said their planned economic and monetary union (EMU) would help to boost job creation and saw "clear grounds for optimism" about economic growth and employment.

"Macroeconomic developments in the form of low inflation, fiscal consolidation, lower interest rates and improving confidence levels and investment profitability are all creating the conditions for increased growth and employment," they said.
"EMU and the euro will make an important contribution to generating the stable macroeconomic framework necessary for sustainable employment," the declaration added.

It called for enhanced labour market efficiency, more "employment friendly" taxation and social protection systems, efforts to modernise goods and services markets and steps to boost Europe's competitiveness.

Implicitly rejecting criticism that austerity programmes aimed at qualifying for EMU were exacerbating unemployment, the leaders added, "There is no conflict between sound macroeconomic and budget policies on the one hand and strong and sustainable growth in output and employment on the other."

It said that although the primary responsibility for fighting unemployment rested with member states, "the Union must support to the fullest extent their efforts to promote employment and minimise unemployment."
